title: Give to United Way's Nepal flood relief fund in Palm Beach | Editorial - Palm Beach Daily News
description: Give to United Way's Nepal flood relief fund in Palm Beach | Editorial  Palm Beach Daily News
publisher.title: Palm Beach Daily News
full_article:
Flash-flooding in northern Nepal has caused widespread destruction, sweeping away people, vehicles, and homes.

The Town of Palm Beach United Way has established a Nepal Recovery Fund to aid those affected by the disaster.

A $100,000 matching grant from the Cathleen McFarlane Foundation will double all donations to the fund.

As of early September, the disaster has resulted in over 1,250 reported deaths and more than 4,750 missing people.

The horror of the videos in northern Nepal is shockingly palpable. A massive wall of muddy water and debris slams down roadways, sweeps away people and vehicles, rips houses from their foundations and transforms rivers into turbulent, deadly menaces.

That the destruction from the flash-flooding has resonated with many Palm Beachers 8,500 miles away isn't surprising. Experience has taught them to fear the power of water unleashed.

And while the threats from hurricanes and storm surges are infinitely different from what happened Aug. 26 in Nepal, the destruction seemed all too familiar. The scenes recalled the horrific aftermath of hurricanes Dorian in the Bahamas and Ian on the west coast of Florida, along with other violent storms that have torn through Florida towns and cities over the years.

Palm Beachers, who for years have largely been spared the wrath of a major hurricane, have learned to say: It could have been us.

Perhaps that's one of the reasons that people are responding with donations to a newly announced fund administered by the Town of Palm Beach United Way to help those affected by the destruction in Nepal. The fund is similar to others the organization has overseen after natural disasters.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

Announced Sept. 1, the Nepal Recovery Fund was kickstarted by a $100,000 matching grant from the West Palm Beach-based Cathleen McFarlane Foundation, named for the late philanthropist who for years lived in Palm Beach. All donations will be matched dollar-for-dollar up to $100,000.

“We have been incredibly encouraged by the response from our community in just the first few days of the Nepal Recovery Fund,” Richard Rothschild, board chair of the Town of Palm Beach United Way, said in a Sept. 3 statement to Palm Beach Daily News .

“We have already received substantial donations, but need additional help to meet the full match by the Cathleen McFarlane Foundation. We are deeply grateful to everyone who has given, and we hope others will join us so we can provide even greater support to families who are facing unimaginable circumstances.”

The human toll of the disaster speaks for itself. As of Sept. 3, more than 4,750 people were missing along miles of Nepal's Bhotekoshi river system and part of neighboring China. Among the missing are more than 600 tourists, including Americans. Over 1,250 deaths had been reported across the region as of Sept. 3, according to reporting by ABC news.

Those numbers are likely to increase as recovery efforts continue.

Money collected through the Town of United Way's relief fund will go to vetted emergency relief organizations to help provide food, clean water, medical care, emergency supplies, shelter and other critically needed essential resources to the communities affected by the tragic event, according to the organization.

Donations can be made online at PalmBeachUnitedWay.org or by writing a check made payable to Town of Palm Beach United Way with "Nepal Fund" in the memo. Checks may be mailed or hand-delivered to the United Way office at 44 Cocoanut Row, Suite M201, Palm Beach, FL 33480. Details about the fund are available by calling the United Way office at 561-655-1919.

Give generously.

title: Nepal flood survivor’s family in China relieved after days of anxious waiting - AP News
description: Nepal flood survivor’s family in China relieved after days of anxious waiting  AP News
publisher.title: AP News
full_article:
HONG KONG (AP) — After days of waiting anxiously, Lu Haitao’s family could finally breathe a sigh of relief when the Chinese man was rescued from a tunnel in Nepal where devastating floods killed more than 1,300 people.

Rescuers carried out Lu from a 225-meter (740-foot) hydropower tunnel and evacuated him by helicopter Saturday, 10 days after the floods. He was taken to a hospital and was in stable condition, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported.

The Aug. 26 floods were likely caused by a glacier collapse, and nearly 4,900 remain missing in the South Asian country, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

Lu recalled climbing to the highest point inside the tunnel and thinking the whistles he heard from the rescue crews were in his imagination, according to audio shared by CCTV. He told a Chinese embassy staffer that the emergency personnel initially could not hear him when he shouted toward their lights.

“When they shone before my eyes, I couldn’t believe it,” he said. “I no longer shouted. I had lost hope.”

Lu Hairong, Lu’s sister in China, told state media Red Star News that she received a call about the rescue before the news emerged. But she only found it believable after seeing him in a picture in the news.

Her 49-year-old brother, who is married with a son, was previously a farmer from Henan province in central China and took additional work, mainly carpentry, during his spare time. He headed to Nepal for work with a fellow villager in February, his first time working abroad, she told Red Star News.

On Saturday, Lu’s cousin received a picture from his sister asking her to help confirm his identity. The man looked very similar but she needed to call another relative to help confirm, the report said.

description: UN's Nepal chief makes emotional plea for flood-ravaged country  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
The United Nations chief in Nepal issued an emotional plea for aid on Sunday, saying survivors of the catastrophic flooding had seen their lives transformed in just "one to two minutes".

After visiting battered mountain communities, UN Resident Coordinator Lila Pieters Yahia told AFP that people were struggling to comprehend how suddenly their Himalayan homes had become an expanse of ruin and destruction.

"You lose your home, you lose your livelihood, you lose your loved one and you lose the breadwinner of your family," Pieters Yahia said in Kathmandu.

"And you know, this happened in one to two minutes."

The devastating August 26 flood that crashed through the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,384 people and left more than 5,500 missing across both countries.

More than 800 foreigners from at least 34 countries are among those missing in both Nepal and Tibet in China. They include both tourists and pilgrims.

Many communities near the epicentre of the disaster remain cut off, with the UN working alongside Nepal's government to get emergency supplies into devastated areas.

The UN has launched a $50 million appeal to help more than 84,000 people affected by the disaster.

"Those people are cut off from the rest of the world because the road is gone," Pieters Yahia said.

"You try to find a solution to expedite access, and you find another bottleneck. We're looking into all means, but we need to to improve access."

- 'Risk of cholera' -

Floods tore through mountain districts, destroying roads, bridges and hydropower dams.

The destruction means journeys that once took a couple of hours have now become day-long ordeals.

"The Himalayas are beautiful, they are amazing, they're spiritual," said Pieters Yahia.

"But also they are very, very difficult terrains... And we have the landslides -- and, plus we're still in the monsoon season."

She warned that beyond immediate shelter and food needs, authorities would have to guard against disease outbreaks and work to protect vulnerable women and girls.

Citing government data, she said 5,000 cattle had died in the flooding.

"This is a big issue because this could lead to communicable diseases... We may have risk of cholera, so this is why immediately we have to invest in sanitation and hygiene."

Pieters Yahia called for greater international support for Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people with limited resources.

"My plea to the international community is: this is the time to help Nepal. It's not tomorrow and it's not yesterday," she said.

"We can't leave them there. We can't leave them alone."

title: China, Nepal race to find thousands still missing 12 days after floods - Al Jazeera
description: China, Nepal race to find thousands still missing 12 days after floods  Al Jazeera
publisher.title: Al Jazeera
full_article:
Rescuers in Nepal are racing to reach thousands of people missing in areas near the China border after catastrophic floods as search operations enter their 12th day.

The flooding that authorities say was likely caused by a glacial collapse last month has killed at least 1,384 people and left more than 5,500 missing, among them about 800 foreigners, across the two countries.

In Nepal, rescuers have retrieved 1,341 bodies and are searching for about 4,996 people, the national disaster agency said on Sunday. In Tibet, the death toll has risen to 43, with 519 people missing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.

Four people have been found alive since Friday, three of them in tunnels at hydropower facilities, where the government initially said about 100 people could be alive. Nepal’s Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said teams at flooded hydropower tunnels were facing multiple challenges.

“Search and rescue is going on at the tunnels despite geography, adverse weather and lack of connectivity,” he told the AFP news agency.

On the Chinese side, rescuers face deep mud, poor weather and the risk of further landslides that have slowed work in the narrow gorge.

Nothing remains of a five-storey customs building at Gyirong, once China’s main land port with Nepal, where workers are digging with shovels, excavators and ground-penetrating radar to recover lost people.

The only road into Gyirong reopened on Wednesday, allowing heavy equipment in.

A case of climate justice

Nepal has issued a request that an untested climate emergency mechanism provide aid.

Advertisement

It is asking the United Nations-backed Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage – founded in 2022 to assist developing countries “particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change” – to cover some of the staggering costs of the flood.

The United Nations has appealed for $50m to help more than 84,000 people, saying the destruction makes delivering aid an immense challenge.

On Wednesday, Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal pointed to the role of leading greenhouse gas emitters that have a “historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal”.

He added that the government has officially filed a “formal climate compensation claim letter” to international partners.

While the exact cause of the glacial collapse remains under investigation, experts say that the frequency and scale of glacier floods have increased as global temperatures have risen.

A United Nations study found that such floods have become nearly five times more frequent since 1950.

Manjeet Dhakal, lead adviser to the UN Least Developed Countries Group on Climate Change, says the global community has a responsibility to cover the cost of disasters afflicting developing nations like Nepal, and that the fund should accept the request.

Countries hit by such disasters are being forced to divert money set aside for health, education and development, he told Al Jazeera. “There are many cases where vulnerable countries are bearing their own cost,” Dhakal said.

The flood was “not caused because of what Nepal has done in the past or in current form”, Dhakal said, noting, “That’s where the global community has a bigger responsibility to come in.”

The UN fund has limited resources, he said. Indeed, its website reflects that it has received only about $631m of $822m in funds pledged by contributing states since inception, and has yet to spend out of the amount.

But, Dhakal said, even a “symbolic amount” could serve as an “inspiring lesson for the fund to justify what it was established for”.

A flood of emotion

Al Jazeera’s Nicolas Haque, reporting from a Buddhist monastery turned shelter in Kathmandu, said refugees there are still only just beginning to reckon with the trauma of the catastrophe.

“There are people meditating, praying, and there are children. It looks like there is a semblance of normal life,” Haque said. “But make no mistake, I was talking to some of the children here. They’ve lost everything. They’ve lost their families, their homes, their parents.”

About 200 people were brought by helicopter to the holy site, known as the Yellow Monastery, where doctors and volunteers have attended to them.

Advertisement

Haque spoke to a volunteer who had put out drawings for children to express their feelings.

“All of them put their stickers on ‘happy’, he said. Now why is that? The reason, he said, is that the children’s emotions remain suppressed so soon after the crisis,” Haque noted.

“What this volunteer told me is that in the days, months, or years to come, the floods will open, just like the floods open in the Himalayas, and emotions will be poured out.”

बुधदिन नेपाल के विदेश मंत्री शिसिर खनाल ग्रीनहाउस गैस उत्सर्जक के अग्रणी के भूमिका दिस इशारा केलखिन्ह जेकरा पर “नेपाल सन कमजोर राष्ट्र के मुआवजा देबय के ऐतिहासिक जिम्मेदारी” अछि.

हुनी आरू कहलकै कि सरकार नँ आधिकारिक तौर प अंतरराष्ट्रीय भागीदारौ क “औपचारिक जलवायु मुआवजा दावा पत्र” दाखिल करलकै ।

हिमनदी केरऽ पतन केरऽ सही कारण केरऽ जांच जारी छै, लेकिन विशेषज्ञऽ के कहना छै कि वैश्विक तापमान बढ़ला के साथ ही ग्लेशियर केरऽ बाढ़ केरऽ आवृत्ति आरू पैमाना बढ़ी गेलऽ छै ।

संयुक्त राष्ट्र केरऽ एगो अध्ययन म॑ पता चललै कि 1950 स॑ ही ऐसनऽ बाढ़ लगभग पांच गुना अधिक होय गेलऽ छै ।

जलवायु परिवर्तन पर संयुक्त राष्ट्र केरऽ अल्पविकसित देश समूह केरऽ प्रमुख सलाहकार मंजीत ढकाल के कहना छै कि नेपाल जैसनऽ विकासशील देशऽ क॑ परेशान करै वाला आपदा केरऽ खर्च पूरा करै के जिम्मेदारी वैश्विक समुदाय के छै, आरू कोष क॑ ई आग्रह क॑ स्वीकार करना चाहियऽ ।

अल जजीरा स॑ बातचीत म॑ हुनी कहलकै कि ऐसनऽ आपदा स॑ प्रभावित देशऽ क॑ स्वास्थ्य, शिक्षा आरू विकास लेली अलग करलऽ गेलऽ पैसा क॑ मोड़ै लेली मजबूर करलऽ जाय रहलऽ छै । ढकल कहलनि जे, बहुत एहन मामला अछि जतय कमजोर देश अपन खर्चा उठा रहल अछि।

बाढ़ि “नेपाल पहिने जे काज केलक अछि या वर्तमान रूप मे केलक ओकर कारण नहि भेल”, ढकाल कहलनि, “ओतहि वैश्विक समुदाय के आबय के पैघ जिम्मेदारी अछि.”

ओ कहला जे संयुक्त राष्ट्र क कोष मे सीमित संसाधन अछि। दरअसल, एकरऽ वेबसाइट स॑ पता चलै छै कि ओकरा शुरू स॑ ही योगदान दै वाला राज्यऽ द्वारा प्रतिज्ञा करलऽ गेलऽ ८२२ मिलियन डॉलर केरऽ फंड म॑ स॑ मात्र लगभग ६३१ मिलियन डॉलर मिललऽ छै, आरू अभी तलक ओकरा ई राशि स॑ बाहर खर्च नै करलऽ गेलऽ छै ।

लेकिन, ढकल न॑ कहलकै कि एगो “सांकेतिक राशि” भी “कोष लेली एगो प्रेरणादायक पाठ के रूप म॑ काम करी सकै छै कि ई कोष क॑ जायज ठहराबै के काम करलऽ जाय कि ओकरऽ स्थापना की लेली करलऽ गेलऽ छै” ।

भावुक बाढ़ि

काठमांडू केरऽ बौद्ध मठ स॑ आश्रय देलऽ गेलऽ अल जजीरा केरऽ निकोलस हक न॑ कहलकै कि वहाँ के शरणार्थी अभी भी प्रलय केरऽ आघात के हिसाब लगाना शुरू करी रहलऽ छै ।

हक कहलनि जे, लोक ध्यान करैत छथि, प्रार्थना करैत छथि, आ बच्चा सेहो अछि, लगैत अछि जेना सामान्य जीवनक आभास अछि। “मुदा गलती नहि करू, हम एत’क किछु बच्चा सभ सँ गप्प क’ रहल छलहुँ, सब किछु गमा लेलक, परिवार, घर, माता-पिता केँ गमा लेलक।”

लगभग 200 लोगऽ क॑ हेलीकॉप्टर स॑ ई पवित्र स्थल प॑ लानलऽ गेलै, जेकरा पीला मठ के नाम स॑ जानलऽ जाय छै, जहां डॉक्टर आरू स्वयंसेवक न॑ हुनकऽ देखभाल करी चुकलऽ छै ।

विज्ञापन

हक एकटा स्वयंसेवक स गप केलथि जे बच्चा सब लेल ड्राइंग लगा क अपन भावना व्यक्त केने छलाह।

ओ कहलनि जे, सब अपन स्टिकर ‘हैप्पी’ पर लगा देलनि। आब से किएक? हुनकऽ कहना छै कि एकरऽ कारण ई छै कि संकट के बाद भी बच्चा सिनी के भावना एतना जल्दी दबाय देलऽ जाय छै,’’ हक न॑ नोट करलकै ।

“ई स्वयंसेवक हमरा जे कहलक से ई जे आबै बला दिन, महीना, वा साल मे बाढ़ि खुजत, ठीक ओहिना जेना हिमालय मे बाढ़ि खुजत, आ भाव उझलि जायत।”
